🐉🔥 Apparently, asking questions before quitting your job is “too much.”

Recently, a company co-founder offered me ₹45,000/month for a work-from-home role — 10 hours a day, 6 days a week — and expected me to leave my current job.

Before making that decision, I asked for clarity.

Not unreasonable demands.

Basic questions.

Is this employment or a contract?

Would I ever be required to travel to the office?

What is the legal company name and office address?

How will TDS/PF/ESI work?

When is salary credited?

What are the working hours, overtime rules, leave policy, probation and notice period?

Who provides the laptop and paid AI/video tools?

Can I continue occasional freelance/promotional work and my own social-media projects outside office hours?

How will my performance be evaluated?

In total, I asked 14 questions.

And that became the problem.

The tone changed.

The irritation became obvious.

The conversation became increasingly informal and dismissive simply because I wanted clarity before resigning from an existing job.

So I declined the offer.

🐉🔥

Here is something hiring companies need to understand:

An offer is not a favour being granted to a candidate.

If you are asking someone to resign from their existing employment and commit most of their week to your company, they have every right to understand exactly what they are signing up for.

Questions about salary, workload, leave, contracts, equipment, outside work and evaluation are not signs of a “difficult employee.”

They are signs of an informed professional.

In fact, if reasonable questions irritate an employer before Day 1, that reaction itself provides useful information about what Day 100 might look like.

Candidates should evaluate employers too.

Have you ever had an employer become uncomfortable simply because you asked detailed questions before accepting an offer? 🐉🔥

Belakangan ini, saya semakin resah melihat pasar kerja Legal. Lowongan terasa semakin terbatas, sementara sebagian perusahaan seolah menganggap fungsi Legal bukan kebutuhan penting. Barangkali, pekerjaan Legal dianggap cukup sederhana,  kontrak bisa dibuat divisi lain, dokumen dapat dibantu AI, dan persoalan hukum bisa diserahkan kepada pihak luar. Jika semua dianggap bisa ditangani tanpa tim Legal, tak heran keberadaannya mulai dipandang sebagai biaya yang bisa dipangkas.

Anggapan itu semakin menarik ketika melihat praktik di lapangan. Dari cerita sejumlah rekan yang bekerja di perusahaan tanpa tim Legal, kontrak ditangani Sales atau Finance, sedangkan somasi kepada vendor diurus HR atau Finance. Ditambah pengalaman saya menjadi mentor kelas Contract Drafting juga menunjukkan bahwa sekitar 80% peserta berasal dari luar bidang hukum, mayoritas Sales dan Finance, disusul beberapa peserta HR. Tentu, siapa pun boleh belajar menyusun kontrak. Namun, ketika pekerjaan Legal semakin mudah dialihkan, muncul pertanyaan yang lebih mendasar " apakah perusahaan hanya membutuhkan dokumennya, atau juga membutuhkan orang yang memahami risiko di baliknya?

Pertanyaan itu penting karena dokumen yang selesai belum tentu menghasilkan perlindungan hukum. Kontrak bisa terlihat rapi, tetapi klausul yang luput dianalisis justru dapat menimbulkan persoalan di kemudian hari. AI dapat membantu menyusun dokumen, tetapi tidak otomatis menggantikan pertimbangan hukum yang mempertimbangkan konteks dan risiko bisnis. 

Karena itu, tantangannya bagi Seorang Legal,bukan hanya mempertahankan kompetensi yg dimiliki melainkan meningkatkan nilai kontribusinya. Kompetensi teknis seperti Legal Due Diligence (LDD), Legal Audit, dan sertifikasi Contract Drafting (CCD) merupakan fondasi penting, tetapi tidak cukup jika Legal tidak mengembangkan pemahaman strategi bisnis dan manajemen risiko. Tanpa kemampuan tersebut, Legal berisiko hanya menjadi pemeriksa dokumen yang menunjukkan apa yang salah, tetapi tidak mampu menjelaskan dampaknya atau menawarkan alternatif kepada manajemen. Jika kontribusinya berhenti pada pekerjaan yang bisa dialihkan ke divisi lain atau dibantu AI, jangan heran jika keberadaannya terus dianggap tidak penting .

Namun, peningkatan kompetensi juga harus diimbangi dengan cara perusahaan menempatkan dan melihat fungsi Legal.
Ditambah dengan budaya anggapan bahwa aspek legal bisa clear asal ada uangnya. Padahal, uang tidak bisa menghapus tanggung jawab hukum dan kepatuhan hukum. 

Pada akhirnya, tidak semua fungsi Legal bisa dialihkan ke divisi lain serta AI dan tidak semua persoalan hukum bisa diselesaikan dengan uang. 
Jangan Hiring Legal kalo hanya untuk formalitas semata.
Dan jangan hiring Legal hanya untuk Print serta Stample Dokumen.
Hiring Legal untuk menjadi bagian strategi bisnis dan managemen risiko perusahaanmu.

If you freelance from Nigeria and get paid in dollars, one rule changed on January 1, 2026 that most freelance advice hasn't caught up with.
Nigerian tax residents are now taxed on worldwide income, including foreign freelance earnings from platforms like Upwork and Fiverr.
(Confirm your own situation with the Nigeria Revenue Service or a licensed accountant. But "nobody checks foreign income" is no longer a safe assumption.)
That was one of five findings from researching a guide for beginner freelancers outside the major Western markets:
1. PayPal now works in Nigeria through a Paga partnership (January 2026). Advice saying it doesn't is outdated.
2. Generic AI task work is growing in volume but paying less per contract. Upwork's 2026 research found volume up about 90% while pay per contract fell 13%. Knowing ChatGPT is not a moat.
3. AI tools confidently invent facts about real people and companies. OpenAI's own testing found its reasoning models got person-specific questions wrong roughly a third to half the time. Verify before you put a "personalized" fact in a pitch.
4. Location bias in freelance hiring is measured, not imagined. Published research found it, and also found that verified proof helps, though it doesn't fully close the gap.
5. Needing the work does not mean you should quote low. Research on negotiation found that a weak fallback offer drags your opening number down more than having no alternative at all.
I put these into a 20-chapter guide: The First International Client System. Every chapter ends with its sources, and where my own checking caught an error, the correction stays visible in the text.
It does not promise clients or income. It gives you a process: validate the problem, build proof, earn trust, price, pitch, contract, get paid.

Why I can't get over it?
Because I found quite alarming how this is not spoken out and how many candidates are suffering in silence. 

‼️ And we see the tendencies when the super cool candidates who get into training contracts, after they qualify, they leave the field, or they mock the companies which give them a stable living. 

Rather than allowing the people who would honour the opportunity provided to them, and for sure will never turn their back to the hand what's feeding them, nooooo they choose the opportunistic perfect assessments holder neurotypical candidates who on the first occasion will leave without any reminiscent. Isn't it funny, sarcastic? 
I think not many have thought about this. 


Are we fully aware that 76% of neurodivergent legal professionals hide their condition from employers because they fear of discrimination, and 74% found the general legal sector non-inclusive based on The Law Society, Law Gazette published on 3rd of May 2024 by John Hyde. 


Some companies are part of The Legal Neurodiversity Network (LNN) and still on purpose changes: 

➡️ the assessments from practice to live one, when the practice one should mirror entirely the live one.

➡️ shouldn't introduce unexpected attention distracting barriers that impact executive functioning ability, which on the practice assessment were not.

Under Equality Act 2010, the entire assessment process must be adjusted to ensure it does not place a disable or neurodiverse candidate at a substantial disadvantage compared to neurotypical candidates. 

By changing the structural pattern of the questions (moving from 8 focused answers to a rapid 2-answer cycle), that were completely absent from the practice environment, and introducing long, disruptive interruption by which the allocated majority of time is spend by reading the disruptive text, (when if you're practiced enough should be already known what and how to do). With this "small change they fundamentally altered the cognitive load required to complete the assessment. 

This structural pattern shift of fragmented abrupt cycles when is told that the practice one is mirrored on the live ones (should be 1 statement to 2 outputs/focus type, not reassured that the live one will be 1 statement to 8 outputs/focus type) which are clearly set out to dismiss a neurodiverse candidates under the fake mask: "we are opened for everyone." Cute.

A recruiter sent me a role this week that has stayed with me. It was a three month contract, described as guaranteed through the end of the year, with the possibility of extension if the person proved their value. Inside the description were three different jobs: someone to build and ship hands-on data and integration work, someone to independently review the architecture and governance of an AI strategy, and someone to write the enterprise roadmap for the year ahead.

Any one of those is a real engagement. Together they describe a hope more than a role.

What interests me is the system that produces a posting like this. When an organization has not yet decided what it actually needs, the ambiguity has to land somewhere, and it usually lands on the person hired to absorb it. The word guaranteed sits beside the phrase prove your value, and the risk quietly moves from the company to the contractor. Nobody in the chain is acting badly. The structure is simply doing what it was built to do.

The better question for any organization is what outcome it wants and which of the three jobs comes first. Build, assess, and plan are different kinds of work, and they deserve to be scoped, sequenced, and paid as such. Clarity at the beginning costs very little, and its absence tends to get billed later in some other form.

This is what is wrong with our world right now. People are struggling to find jobs, and too many companies are taking advantage of that.

I passed on this one, kindly. If you are hiring for something like it, start by separating the jobs.

Layoffs are down 41%.

Hiring is back to 2013 levels.

Both are true. Only one makes the headlines.

The numbers:
→ Announced job cuts through August: down 41% (Challenger, Gray & Christmas)
→ Hiring rate: 3.3%, roughly where it was in 2013 (BLS JOLTS)
→ Quit rate: 1.9%. People with jobs aren't leaving.
→ Job openings: a five-month low in August
→ #1 reason given for cuts this year: AI. 116,175 jobs, 22% of the total.

Economists call this a "low-hire, low-fire" market.

Picture a building with a locked front door. Almost no one is being pushed out. Almost no one is getting in.

The Cleveland Fed found those hit hardest are job seekers who aren't currently employed. That's why the jobs report and your search feel like two different economies.

This is the Great Restructuring.

Companies aren't just cutting. They're redesigning how work gets done:
→ Fewer full-time roles
→ More contract and project-based work
→ Flatter teams with fewer managers
→ Budget moved from headcount to AI

Why? In a UK survey of 1,000+ business leaders, 39% have scaled back full-time hiring. Their top reasons: flexibility (49%) and avoiding long-term commitments (43%). Only 34% said cost.

It's not just about saving money. It's about never being locked in again.

Where the cuts are concentrated this year:
→ Technology: 155,126, nearly 30% of all cuts
→ Transportation: up 271% from 2025

The cost no jobs report measures:
For candidates:
→ Hundreds of applications, very few replies
→ Savings shrinking while the search stretches on
→ Starting to doubt skills that were in demand two years ago

For employees who still have jobs:
→ Survivor's guilt after watching colleagues get cut
→ Absorbing that work with no added pay or title
→ Staying in roles they'd leave if they could
→ Using AI tools they fear will replace them
→ Watching contractors do the same work and wondering if they're next
→ Quietly pulling back, because loyalty no longer feels safe

Keeping your job in this market doesn't mean you're okay.

For recruiters and hiring managers:
→ Hundreds of applicants per opening, no time to answer most
→ Saying no to good people every day
→ Doing more with fewer people while their own roles feel uncertain

Everyone in this market is carrying more than they say out loud.

If you're job searching:
→ Contract work is often the way in now. Don't dismiss it.
→ Search every version of your title. Many have been renamed.
→ Referrals matter more when openings are scarce
→ A long search in this market is not a verdict on your ability

If you're hiring:
→ Close the loop. A rejection email takes 30 seconds and is remembered for years.
→ Check in on your team. The people who stayed are carrying more.

Job seekers: how long has your current search taken?

Employees: what's changed most at work this year?

Recruiters: are you seeing more contract reqs than full-time?

Today’s Pulse:

The biggest workforce story this week isn’t a layoff.

The U.S. has suspended PERM processing for Microsoft, Adobe and several major IT-services firms, including Infosys, TCS, Wipro and Cognizant.

PERM is a key step in employer-sponsored permanent residency. Suspending it creates uncertainty for affected foreign workers and limits an important recruitment and retention pathway for these companies.

It doesn’t mean existing employees have lost their jobs, nor does it automatically cancel their work visas. But it raises a bigger question: How will technology companies secure specialized talent if access to international hiring becomes more restricted?

Meanwhile, Amazon continues cutting corporate roles while CloudBees expands U.S. hiring.

The signal: AI is changing the skills companies need, while immigration policy is changing how they can access those skills.

• Immigration restrictions could reshape tech talent strategies.
• Domestic hiring and reskilling may become more important.
• Workforce policy can be as consequential as layoffs.

What a room. Nearly 50 people packed into AI House in Seattle for our October event, and even more joined online. We even had Winston Mariku join us live from Kenya, across eleven time zones! YAY!  

The news roundup with Freya Yu We shared community news: our stewardship of the OVERT.AI standard, our AI governance work with the University of Washington on healthcare, and our new Product Feedback Forum, opening soon. Then Freya ran through the headlines with me. 

Angela Wu: Words matter
Angela graciously spoke at the event. Anything she shared was her own opinions and did not reflect onions from her client. Angela was my legal counsel at Microsoft. Her advice was straight forward. 

Drop the absolutes. 100% safe sets a bar you'll never clear. Say helps ensure. Regulators read what you said publicly at the time. She proved it with one letter to a funeral home that got a family $13,000 back. Ha! 

Open source isn't always free, and some models are research-only. Mark attorney emails privileged, and for crazy ideas, pick up the phone. (Don't put that in email, Ken.) Her single guardrail? Talk to your lawyer. 

Aaron Rieke: The law is already here Aaron, founder of Privlex and a former FTC advisor, joined from DC. The FTC bans unfair and deceptive practices, and those two big words already cover a lot of AI. Don't wait for a federal AI law. His Rite Aid example showed a 100-year-old law handling bad facial recognition just fine. 

My favorite line: when executives ask how the law will hold AI agents accountable, he says sweet summer child. Courts don't come for the model. They come for your company. 

Heather Zindel, CEO of AIMonster.ai, asked whether hallucinations are on the LLM provider. Aarons answer was mostly bad news. Liability lands on deployers, and the labs contracts describe a giant word slot machine. On Mobley v. Workday, his advice was to do bias testing on real outcomes, with a lawyer involved so the findings stay privileged. 

The audience stole the show 
A former Microsoft designer argued for hiring design researchers alongside lawyers. Aaron backed that up with Amazons Prime signup flow, which the business team nicknamed Project Iliad. (Oh my gosh.) Hire the designers, then listen to them. Trey asked if I didnt know holds up legally. Aaron: tough cookies. And an AI detector said my 100% human writing was 87% AI. Angela thinks I'm turning into one. 

Thank you's and what's next 
Thanks to Angela, Aaron, Bob R., our stewards Corey Scherrer, Stacy Tatem, Freya Yu, and Bill Anderson, AI House, and Karen and Chris Jones for the group photo. 

Next month: AI insurability. January: AI and healthcare. And Seattle's own AI Con USA wants speakers by Oct 18. I'm reviewing the governance track. 

See you next month!

The federal government spends more than $100 billion a year on IT, and about 80% of it goes to keeping existing systems running. GAO’s July 2025 report put that at roughly $83 billion in FY2025 across 24 agencies.

States don’t publish their version of this number, but there’s no reason to think theirs would look much different.

When you build in house, launch day isn’t the finish line. Everything that comes after it becomes somebody’s permanent job. Someone has to pass the security review every year, pull the audit trail when a records request comes in, answer for data handling when the contract gets tested, and train the next two hundred people who join.

At the same time, the people who know how those systems work are leaving. In NASCIO’s 2026 State CIO Survey, the biggest workforce concern wasn’t hiring developers. It was that the people who carry the institutional knowledge behind existing systems are retiring, there aren’t many people coming up behind them, and AI is changing what an IT role even looks like.

That’s the part of build vs buy that rarely makes it into the business case. A statewide rulemaking system isn’t a project with an end date. It touches every agency, runs for a decade or more, and usually outlasts the administration that approved it. The build ends up being the shortest part of the whole commitment.

The federal number is published. Most states would have to go find theirs. What share of your state’s IT budget is already committed to keeping existing systems running, who owns the ones built in-house once the original team moves on, and does that plan hold for the next ten years?

→ Retention becomes about culture and growth, not contracts

If you're a CTO, now's a good time to ask: would your best people stay if they were free to leave tomorrow?

The most fragile part of your supply chain in 2026 is not the warehouse, the carrier, or the supplier. It is the gap between a demand signal you trust and a procurement action you can take.

I have been building the middleware that connects real-time demand sensing with production scheduling for teams trying to escape the "forecast-to-purchase-order" lag. The non-obvious bottleneck is not the model accuracy. It is the human workflow that sits between the AI recommendation and the purchase order release. Even with a perfect forecast, if the planner has to manually cross-reference three different systems to validate the recommendation, the latency kills any agility.

A trend quietly reshaping the field is the maturation of "digital twins" not for simulation, but for pre-validation. The best teams are no longer running scenarios to guess what might happen. They are using a digital twin of their actual supplier base, inventory positions, and lead times to test every proposed procurement decision before it touches a real contract. This shifts the role of the planner from a validator of recommendations to a designer of constraints. The planner defines the "no-fly zones" — minimum service levels, maximum carbon exposure, acceptable cost variance — and the system handles the rest.

Another shift that is changing the competitive landscape is the rise of contract-aware procurement. The latest trends confirm that disruption is now normalized, and teams need to switch modes instantly. But the reason most teams cannot switch fast is not the logistics. It is the contract layer. When you move from ocean to air, the Incoterms, the liability caps, and the delivery windows all shift. The teams that are winning have embedded their contract terms directly into the procurement workflow, so the system can instantly evaluate the trade-off between expedited cost and contractual risk.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the candidate you need is not the person who can configure an ERP or run a standard forecast. You need someone who has designed the workflow that closes the gap between AI recommendation and procurement action, who understands how to build a digital twin that validates decisions before they are made, and who can encode contract terms as operational constraints. I am actively exploring the next challenge where I can apply these systems-thinking principles to help a team move from reactive replenishment to proactive procurement.

What is the one contract term you have encoded into your procurement system that prevents a costly default decision?
